title: Murmuration runtime handoff — late shift notes
content:
Shift summary (late shift, 03/12 -> 03/13)

Context:
- Saw a recurring p99 token latency spike around 21:40 UTC that propagated across 3 zones. Pattern felt like a 'murmuration' — many short bursts, not a single sustained load.
- Triggered alert INF-2431. Put quick triage in place, left notes here for morning handoff.

Observations:
1) Metrics at spike:
   - CPU on runtime-worker Pods climbed ~30% for 60-90s windows.
   - Avg batch size transiently jumped from 6 -> 18 for gpt-2-medium variant.
   - KV cache hit rate dropped ~12% during windows (possible eviction thrash).
   - NVLink saturation small blips but not sustained.
2) Logs:
   - Error rate did not rise dramatically; most requests succeeded but waited longer on token generation.
   - Found repeated WARN about "kv-cache-miss: key chain-length mismatch" in node-34.
3) Recent changes deployed earlier today: small batching scheduler tweak (PR #987) that raises join-window default from 10ms -> 15ms.

Immediate actions taken (what I did):
- Rolled back PR #987 on canary pool (kubectl apply -f canary-deploy-rollback.yaml). Canary latency returned to baseline within two windows.
- Restarted runtime-worker on node-34 (ssh prod-node-34; sudo systemctl restart runtime-worker). Warnings about kv-cache-miss reduced.
- Scoped tickets: added comment on INF-2431 with timestamps + brief logs.

Hypotheses (ranked):
A) The join-window increase allowed more heterogeneous request mixing -> larger batches where prefix behaviors differ -> KV-cache misses spike -> longer per-token time for deserialization/kv reconcile. (Most likely)
B) Short-lived traffic bursts cause allocation churn at GPU memory allocator leading to tiny GC-like stalls. (possible, lower priority)
C) Network flakiness between nodes caused temporary cache ownership confusion (less evidence).

Quick experiments to run (when you pick this up):
- Reproduce locally with request trace replay: use replay script in infra/tools/replay (arg: --burstiness=high --trace=2026-03-12-2140). Compare batch-size histogram.
- Toggle join-window back and forth on canary (15ms -> 10ms -> 12ms) and observe p99 impact over ~30m windows.
- Increase kv-cache size on node-34 by +25% to see if hits stabilize (patch: runtime-config/kv-cache-node-34.json).

Playbook steps (for SRE/next person):
- If alert fires again: 1) move traffic off the affected pods (kubectl cordon/drain), 2) rollback batching scheduler to 10ms on canary, 3) restart runtime-worker on flagged node, 4) collect /metrics and /proc/gpu stats for 10m.
- If rollback fixes canary but prod still spiky: throttle join-window change rollout and open a rollback to previous commit for prod.

Outstanding notes/questions:
- Need a deterministic way to map request headers -> batch grouping to see if heterogenous prefixes are being co-batched. Maybe add lightweight tagging in the scheduler.
- Confirm whether the join-window change was intended for bursty clients (ask PM: @kai).
- Would quantization profiles affect these micro behavior? Talk to research about token decode overhead differences.

Commands & quick snippets I used:
- kubectl logs -n runtime -l app=runtime-worker --since=2h | grep "kv-cache-miss" | sed -n '1,200p'
- ssh prod-node-34
- sudo systemctl restart runtime-worker
- kubectl apply -f canary-deploy-rollback.yaml -n runtime

Todo (my list before I sign off):
- [x] Roll back canary patch and monitor for 30m.
- [x] Restart node-34 worker.
- [ ] Add replay job for the 21:40 trace and run in staging.
- [ ] Draft a small perf test to vary join-window and measure batch heterogeneity.
- [ ] Follow up with PM on intent of PR #987.

Handoff to morning shift:
- Check INF-2431 — I added timestamps and logs. If it recurs, prioritize replay and kv-cache size bump.
- If you see kv-cache-miss WARNs concentrated on a single node, cordon and replace that node from the pool.

Random quick thoughts (freeform):
- The 'murmuration' metaphor might be useful for explaining these microbursts to non-technical stakeholders — lots of small coordinated motions creating a visible wave.
- Longer-term: consider per-client affinity hints in scheduler to avoid mixing very short contexts with long-running reranks in same batch.

Attachments I left:
- logs/2026-03-12-21-40-node-34.txt (on my workstation)
- replay traces uploaded to s3://redwood-inference/replays/2026-03-12-2140

Pinging: @Evan Holtz for follow-up on rollout controls, @Kai Rivera for product intent.

End of notes.
